previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder with a chronic suprapubic catheter, was admitted for lethargy and found to have severe sepsis from a multidrug-resistant urinary tract infection. Blood and urine cultures grew MDR E. coli and VRE, prompting treatment with daptomycin and meropenem. Imaging revealed an obstructing right kidney stone causing hydronephrosis, requiring percutaneous nephrostomy. He also developed aspiration pneumonia, likely due to impaired swallowing, and was managed with NG tube feeding before passing a swallow study and resuming a pureed diet. An ostomy prolapse was noted but managed conservatively. His condition improved with treatment, renal function normalized, and he was discharged home on a four-week course of IV antibiotics via PICC line, with follow-up planned for stone removal and surgical evaluation.

INDICATION:  ___ with likelky urosepsis, h/o obstructing stones, right
percutaneous nephrostomy tube, evaluate for location of tube, obstructing
stones.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT images of the abdomen and pelvis were acquired
without intravenous contrast. Non-contrast scan has several limitations in
detecting vascular and parenchymal organ abnormalities, including tumor
detection.  Note, patient unable to lie prone.
Coronal and sagittal reformations were performed and reviewed on PACS.
Oral contrast was not administered.

DOSE:  Total DLP (Body) = 881 mGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast ___.

FINDINGS: 

LOWER CHEST: Scattered streaky opacities at the lung bases are compatible with
subsegmental atelectasis; otherwise, the partially imaged lung bases are
clear. There is no pleural or pericardial effusion. There is no hiatus hernia.

CT ABDOMEN:

HEPATOBILIARY: The liver demonstrates a normal homogeneous noncontrast
appearance without apparent focal lesion.  There is no obvious intrahepatic
biliary ductal dilation.  Lack of IV contrast precludes evaluation of the
portal vein.  The gallbladder demonstrates a normal noncontrast appearance
without evidence of surrounding inflammation or radiopaque stones.  There is
no extrahepatic biliary ductal dilation.

PANCREAS: The pancreas is normal in appearance.  There is no peripancreatic
stranding or ductal dilation.

SPLEEN: A 14 mm accessory spleen is seen superiorly.  There is no
splenomegaly.

ADRENALS: The adrenal glands are normal.

URINARY: New since CT performed ___ is mild to moderate left
hydroureteronephrosis.  A dilated left ureter extends to the left UVJ, where a
0.8 cm left UVJ calculus is presumably obstructing.  At least two additional
nonobstructing stones are seen within the bladder lumen measuring 1.1 and 0.5
cm.

A right percutaneous nephrostomy tube is seen in grossly appropriate location.
There is no evidence of kinking or abnormality along the course of the tube,
which exits via the right flank.  Multiple foci of clustered nonobstructing
right renal calculi are relatively unchanged in comparison to prior CT,
measuring 0.9 (series 2, image 30) and 1.2 cm (series 2, image 40).  There is
no right hydronephrosis.

Multiple nonobstructing 0.2-0.3 cm left renal calculi are seen (for example
see series 2, image 34).

The renal parenchyma demonstrates an unremarkable noncontrast appearance
bilaterally

GASTROINTESTINAL: The stomach and duodenum are unremarkable.  A single
prominent, distended loop of small bowel measuring up to 2.8 cm, otherwise,
there is no evidence of obstruction, wall thickening, or other small bowel
abnormality.  The patient is status post sigmoid resection with a right lower
quadrant end-colostomy.  The rectal stump is unremarkable.  The colostomy site
is normal in appearance.  The colon is filled with stool, and otherwise
unremarkable.

VASCULAR AND LYMPH NODES: Mildly prominent left periaortic retroperitoneal
lymph nodes measure up to 8 mm in short axis, not pathologically enlarged by
CT size criteria, likely reactive in nature.  There is no mesenteric
lymphadenopathy.  There is no free intraperitoneal air or fluid.

CT PELVIS:
A suprapubic tube is seen entering the bladder via the right anterior abdomen,
as on prior.  Mild diffuse bladder wall thickening may relate at least
partially to underdistention, possibly in addition to a component of chronic
inflammation, overall unchanged appearance since ___.  Multiple small
intraluminal foci of gas layering anti dependently within the bladder lumen
are not unexpected in the setting of catheterization.  The distal right ureter
is unremarkable.  There is no pelvic sidewall, iliac chain, or inguinal
lymphadenopathy.  There is no free pelvic fluid.

MUSCULOSKELETAL: There is diffuse osseous demineralization.  There is moderate
dextroscoliosis centered at L1.  No concerning focal lytic or sclerotic
osseous lesions are identified.

IMPRESSION:


1. 0.8 cm obstructing left UVJ calculus resulting in new mild to moderate left
hydroureteronephrosis.
2. Multiple bilateral, right greater than left nonobstructing renal calculi
measuring up to 1.2 cm.
3. At least 2 additional nonobstructing bladder calculi, measuring up to 1.1
cm.
4. Appropriately positioned and normal-appearing right nephrostomy catheter.
5. Status post sigmoid resection with end colostomy the right lower quadrant. 
Unremarkable rectal stump.
6. Unchanged diffuse mild bladder wall thickening with small intraluminal foci
of gas, not unexpected in the setting of suprapubic catheterization.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with urosepsis and left UVJ stone, obstructing //

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ and Dr.
___ radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
___ supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure
and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
100 mcg of fentanyl and 2 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 47 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS:  Cefalexin 1 g IV
CONTRAST: 15 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 2.09 min, 5 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Left ultrasound guided renal collecting system access.
2. Left nephrostogram.
3. Percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
prone on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The left flank was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

After the injection of 5 cc of 1% lidocaine in the subcutaneous soft tissues,
the left renal collecting system was accessed through a posterior lower pole
calyx under ultrasound guidance using a 21 gauge Cook needle. Ultrasound
images of the access were stored on PACS. Prompt return of urine confirmed
appropriate positioning.  Under fluoroscopic guidance, a Nitinol wire was
advanced into the renal collecting system. After a skin ___, the needle was
exchanged for an Accustick sheath. Once the tip of the sheath was in the
collecting system; the sheath was advanced over the wire, inner dilator and
metallic stiffener. The wire and inner dilator were then removed and diluted
contrast was injected into the collecting system to confirm position. An
Amplatz wire was advanced through the sheath and coiled in the collecting
system. The sheath was then removed and an 8 ___ nephrostomy tube was
advanced into the renal collecting system. The wire was then removed and the
pigtail was formed in the collecting system. Contrast injection confirmed
appropriate positioning. The catheter was then flushed, 0 silk stay sutures
applied and the catheter was secured witha Stat Lock device and sterile
dressings. The catheter was attached to a bag.

FINDINGS: 

1. Mild to moderate hydroureteronephrosis, with narrowing of the contrast
column in the distal ureter compatible with partial obstruction from known
left UVJ stone. Contrast progression into the bladder was seen.

2. Left percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement with pigtail in the renal
pelvis.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of an 8 ___ nephrostomy on the left.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  Routine catheter exchange in 3 months if the nephrostomy
catheter remains in place after lithotripsy.

EXAMINATION:  RENAL U.S.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with history of bilateral perc nephrostomies for
obstructive nephrolithiasis, now with decreased urine output on RIGHT side  //
signs of obstruction of RIGHT kidney / perc nephrostomy

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the kidneys were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis ___

FINDINGS: 

The right kidney measures 11.2 cm.  Due to patient discomfort and positioning
the left kidney could not be visualized.  The right kidney shows no
hydronephrosis or mass.  There are several nonobstructing subcentimeter right
renal stones.  The percutaneous nephrostomy is seen in the right renal pelvis.
There is normal cortical echogenicity and corticomedullary differentiation.

The bladder is moderately well distended and contains a Foley catheter and
several dependent stones, one likely within the left ureterovesicular
junction.

IMPRESSION:


1. Percutaneous nephrostomy within the right renal pelvis without
hydronephrosis.
2. Several nonobstructing stones in the right kidney and urinary bladder.
3. Probable obstructing stone at the left UVJ also seen on recent CT.
4. Due to patient discomfort and positioning the left kidney could not be
visualized.
